title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt (June 2025)
summary: AI-generated podcast summary of MIT's 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' EEG study of essay writing with an LLM, search or no tools.

assertions.quote: the LLM to brain group ... their brains did not show that big ramp up in connectivity

verdicts.note: The MIT Media Lab preprint (54 participants, 18 in the crossover) found lower EEG connectivity and poor recall; small, not peer-reviewed at release, and essay-specific, so effects on coding are inference.
Secondhand summary of Kosmyna et al. EEG study (N=54): ChatGPT-assisted essay writers showed lower cognitive activity and worse recall of their work; persistence after tool removal is not mentioned.

For code, this study finds an analogue of the claim: lower recall and explanation of one's own just-written work after AI use. It cites Kosmyna et al. as consistent. Brain engagement and whether the effect persists after the tool is removed were not tested.

assertions.quote: The LLM group's essays on the same topic were statistically much more similar to each other

verdicts.note: Several studies find reduced diversity of ideas and phrasing with LLM assistance (creative writing, ideation); consistent with the MIT result.
Authors speculate that AI assistants homogenize code into standard constructs, citing Haase et al. on LLM output clustering, but do not measure homogeneity themselves.

assertions.quote: reliance on AI for core thinking tasks might lead to those brain circuits being well less developed

verdicts.note: Anthropic's 2026 RCT found AI-assisted learners scored lower on mastery of a new library, and other studies show reduced engagement; effects depend on how AI is used.
The review describes 'cognitive debt': deferring understanding during fast iteration raises later debugging and maintenance costs. It does not measure skill loss directly.
